title: Emberfield - Dedicated GPU Reserve Intake
summary: Introductory discovery where Emberfield outlines production inference needs for a multimodal assistant: expected peak concurrency, strict isolation for regulated customer data, bursty weekly traffic, and a preference for reserved GPUs with warm-pool burst. Discussed tradeoffs hosted vs dedicated vs private, KMS integration, SOC2/audit logs, and realistic latency targets. Agreed to run a short benchmark and follow up with security pack and pricing sheet.
action_items: Alex Morgan - Send Dedicated pricing sheet + reserved tiers - due 2027-11-24
Priya Shah - Share warm-pool prewarm recommendations and benchmark template - due 2027-11-25
Emberfield / Jordan - Provide tokenized request profile (P95 request size, concurrency distribution) - due 2027-11-26
next_steps: Redwood to provide security pack (SOC2 summary, encryption and KMS integration docs)
Schedule a 2-hour benchmark session with Emberfield engineering week of 2027-11-29
Emberfield to confirm internal pilot scope and success metrics (latency, cost per 1k tokens, error rate)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-21
Start time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
---
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. Quick round-robin?
[00:07] Michael (Emberfield): Michael here, VP Eng. We build Ember — multimodal assistant for financial workflows. Sara is our ML lead, Jordan handles infra, Tariq is security, Olivia product.
[00:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Thanks. We'll do intake, try to map constraints (latency, isolation, burst). We'll also sketch out pilots and benchmarks.
[00:26] Sara (Emberfield): High level: we have a mix of text and document OCR models, heavy embeddings for search/rerank. Currently using self-hosted GPUs and a bit of hosted API for spikes. Want a long-term path: reserved GPUs (Dedicated) with strict tenant isolation for certain customers, and a warm-pool for burst.
[00:44] Jordan (Emberfield): Traffic is weird — baseline 30 rps, spikes up to 650 rps for a few hours, mainly during business opens and scheduled batch jobs. We care about P95 latency under 350ms for short prompts (<=512 tokens), and cost-per-token is also a gating factor.
[01:03] Alex (Redwood AE): Got it. Two obvious levers: dedicated pools pinned for isolation, and warm/hot pools for burst prewarming. Curious about what "strict isolation" means for you — separate GPUs per tenant, or VPC/private deployment?
[01:17] Tariq (Emberfield): For top-tier customers and regulated accounts we need hardware separation—no co-tenancy. That could be dedicated nodes per customer or a tenant-fenced reserved pool. We also require KMS integration for model request envelopes and audit logs for every inference call. SOC2 Type II in progress.
[01:33] Priya (Redwood SE): We support Dedicated with tenant fencing and optional node-level isolation in Private deployments. For KMS we integrate with customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-key), and audit logs can be routed to customer S3 or SIEM. Can you run through your model sizes and quantization?
[01:46] Sara (Emberfield): We run a 20B transformer for multimodal fusion and a trimmed 7B for quick responses. 20B will be quantized to int8 in many cases; however some customers demand fp16 for highest quality. Also we use KV cache reuse a lot for multi-turn.
[02:03] Priya (Redwood SE): That matters for memory and packing. For 20B fp16 we need full GPU per model, but int8 allows higher packing and more concurrent sessions. Our runtime supports KV-aware batching, and we can set up route policies so heavy customers land on nodes sized for fp16.
[02:22] Olivia (Emberfield): What about fallback behavior if reserved capacity is saturated during a storm? Is there automatic burst to hosted or degraded quality models?
[02:31] Alex (Redwood AE): Yes — we can define fallback policies: warm-pool scale, canary to a compatible quantized variant, or route to a hosted tier (if acceptable) with explicit SLA tradeoffs. For top-tier regulated customers you can disable cross-tenant fallback.
[02:45] Michael (Emberfield): We probably want a two-level approach: first try warm-pool and prewarmed hot instances, second a quantized variant on same hardware, third only as last resort route to a private-hosted fallback but not to public shared endpoints.
[02:59] Priya (Redwood SE): Makes sense. Are your burst events predictable? You mentioned scheduled batches — we can pre-warm based on cron signals or API weight triggers.
[03:09] Jordan (Emberfield): We have both predictable nightly jobs (batch embeddings) and unpredictable daytime traffic from users. Nightly jobs cause 10x throughput for a 30–45 minute window. We don't want those jobs to evict serving traffic.
[03:22] Priya (Redwood SE): For that pattern we recommend separate capacity pools: a reserved pool for low-latency interactive workloads and a batch-dedicated pool for embedding jobs, with controlled preemption rules. Warm-pools can be configured to keep X GPUs hot for Y minutes after last use.
[03:39] Tariq (Emberfield): Security: we need mutual TLS in the control plane, RBAC with SSO (SAML/Okta), and audit trails. Also clarification on data retention — inference traces might be persisted for up to 90 days for debugging but must be encrypted with customer KMS.
[03:54] Priya (Redwood SE): All supported. Our Private offering can run in your VPC with customer KMS and we support SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC. Audit logs can be redacted and retained to your spec. We'll include our SOC2 artifact in the security pack.
[04:08] Sara (Emberfield): Performance question — what's realistic P95 for a 20B model quantized on a V100/RTX A6000 equivalent? Our latency target is tight.
[04:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Rough numbers: for int8 on an A6000 equivalent, single-stream generation up to 512 tokens tends to be 200–400ms P95 depending on prompt patterns and KV reuse. fp16 will sometimes be slightly faster per token but has more memory constraints and lower packing density. We'll baseline with your prompts.
[04:36] Michael (Emberfield): Cost modeling: we need to compare reserved capacity cost vs on-demand hosted spikes. Can you show unit economics?
[04:44] Alex (Redwood AE): We'll send a pricing grid showing reserved monthly/annual tiers, burst pricing, and a worked example using your request mix. Priya will share the optimize recommendations (batching, prefilling KV) to reduce token unit cost.
[04:58] Jordan (Emberfield): About network: we need egress constraints, VPC peering, and private endpoints — we also want to avoid data leaving our region for compliance.
[05:06] Priya (Redwood SE): We have regional deployments and private control plane options. Dedicated in-region only is configurable. For Private on-prem, we can provide an air-gapped package but that is a heavier lift.
[05:18] Olivia (Emberfield): Pilot scope idea: reserve 4 GPUs for two weeks, run 3 load profiles (baseline, nightly batch, spikes), measure P50/P95, cost per 1k tokens, error rate, plus KMS integration test.
[05:29] Alex (Redwood AE): Sounds good. We'll propose a pilot: 4x A6000-equivalent reserved for 2 weeks, bench three profiles, include warm-pool scenario and quantized-vs-fp16 comparison. We'll also include a runbook for failover policies.
[05:45] Tariq (Emberfield): Who signs off internally? Need security and finance to see numbers. I'll own the security review, Olivia will lead product acceptance, Michael signoff engineering.
[05:55] Alex (Redwood AE): Great. Quick clarifying questions from us: can you share an anonymized request histogram and sample prompts? That lets Priya size batch windows and suggest prefill strategies.
[06:06] Jordan (Emberfield): We'll extract a 48-hour sample and a synthetic spike. Expect to have that by Friday.
[06:12] Priya (Redwood SE): We've seen cases where prefix caching reduces token spend by 20–40% for multi-turn agents — if you can provide dialogues, we can estimate savings.
[06:23] Sara (Emberfield): Noted. Also curious about observability: will we get token-level latency breakdowns, tracing, and per-route dashboards?
[06:32] Alex (Redwood AE): Yes, Redwood Console has per-model/per-route latency and token cost, traces for individual requests, and alerting. We can grant access for 2 week pilot.
[06:42] Michael (Emberfield): Any limitations on GPU types for dedicated — we prefer Ampere but open to A100 if needed.
[06:50] Priya (Redwood SE): We map hardware by SKU. A100 gives more memory and packing — good for fp16 20B. A6000-equivalent is common for int8. We'll include hardware recommendations in the pilot proposal.
[07:03] Olivia (Emberfield): For the test, can you provide a sample playbook for failover? If warm pool fills, we want a hard cap for latency degradation instead of unbounded queues.
[07:12] Priya (Redwood SE): We can implement SLO-step policies: when queue length exceeds threshold, reject low-priority requests, fallback to quantized model, then enable extra burst nodes. We'll draft the playbook.
[07:28] Alex (Redwood AE): To wrap up, recap and next steps?
[07:32] Michael (Emberfield): Recap: Emberfield needs dedicated reserved capacity with hardware isolation for regulated customers, warm-pool burst for spikes, separate batch capacity, KMS and audit integration, pilot to validate latency/cost.
[07:44] Alex (Redwood AE): Redwood to send security pack, pricing grid, pilot proposal with benchmark plan, and warm-pool recommendations. Customer to send traffic samples and confirm pilot signoffs.
[07:54] Olivia (Emberfield): Good. We'll review internally and aim to kick pilot the week of 11/29.
[07:59] Alex (Redwood AE): Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invite and docs.
